newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns rival Taiwan over Dalai Lama visit.
newsitem.headline: China warns rival Taiwan over Dalai Lama visit.

text.p: China on Friday warned Taiwan not to fan separatist sentiment during a visit this month by Tibet's spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, and said the island had strayed from the goal of national unity.
"The Dalai Lama is a political figure in a lengthy exile and is engaged in activities aimed at splitting the motherland," Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said.
"His visit to Taiwan will inevitably have political purposes," Qian told a news conference.
The Dalai Lama, who won the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent campaign for autonomy for his Himalayan homeland, will make a six-day visit to Taiwan beginning on March 22.
Beijing insists that both the exiled Dalai Lama, who fled to India after an abortive uprising against Chinese rule in 1959, and Taiwan's leaders have a pro-independence agenda.
China and Taiwan have been divided since the nationalists fled to the island in 1949 after losing their civil war to the communists on the mainland.
Taiwan's leaders maintain they want reunification with China but only after the mainland has a democratic political system.

"We hope the Taiwan authorities will adopt a prudent and wise attitude (towards the Dalai Lama), and refrain from any actions that are detrimental to the unification of the motherland and to ethnic unity," Qian said.
The Dalai Lama, worshipped as a god-king in Tibet, has said his visit will be purely religious.
Qian said Taiwan had strayed from the goal of reunificiation with the mainland and urged its leaders to return to the principle that the island is part of China.
Beijing has shut down a semi-official channel for talks between the two sides and has given no sign it is ready for a reopening.
"Now they (Taiwan's leaders) simply refuse to mention 'one China', and this has caused significant difficulty for the talks across the two sides," Qian said.
"Under such circumstances, how can direct talks between the two sides be possible?" he asked.
Qian said Beijing hoped for direct communication, transport and trade links between the two sides because such ties would boost economic development.
Taiwan bans direct links with China but allows indirect trade and transport, usually through Hong Kong.
